'''Leslie Eleazer Orgel''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dunitz|first1=Jack D.|last2=Joyce|first2=Gerald F.|date=1 December 2013|title=Leslie Eleazer Orgel. 12 January 1927 – 27 October 2007|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|language=en|volume=59|pages=277–289|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2013.0002|issn=0080-4606|doi-access=free}}</ref> (12 January 1927 – 27 October 2007) was a British [[chemist]] and member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]], known for his theories on the [[origin of life]].

==Biography==
{{refimprove section | date = March 2024}}
Leslie Orgel was born in [[London]] on {{birth date|df=yes|1927|1|12}}. He received his Bachelor of Arts degree in chemistry with [[British undergraduate degree classification#First-class honours|first-class honours]] from the [[University of Oxford]] in 1948. In 1951 he was elected a [[Research fellow|Fellow]] of [[Magdalen College, Oxford]], and in 1953 was awarded his PhD in chemistry.

Orgel started his career as a [[Theoretical chemistry|theoretical]] [[Inorganic chemistry|inorganic]] chemist and continued his studies in this field at Oxford, the [[California Institute of Technology]], and the [[University of Chicago]].

Together with [[Sydney Brenner]], [[Jack D. Dunitz|Jack Dunitz]], [[Dorothy Hodgkin]], and Beryl M. Oughton he was one of the first people in April 1953 to see the model of the structure of [[DNA]], constructed by [[Francis Crick]] and [[James D. Watson|James Watson]], at the time he and the other scientists were working at Oxford University's Chemistry Department.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Eighth Day of Creation: Makers of the Revolution in Biology|last=Judson|first=Horace Freeland|publisher=CSH Press|year=2013|isbn=978-0-879694-78-4|location=Cold Spring Harbor, New York|page=238}}</ref> According to the late Dr. Beryl Oughton, later Rimmer, they all travelled together in two cars once Dorothy Hodgkin announced to them that they were off to Cambridge to see the model of the structure of DNA. All were impressed by the new DNA model, especially Brenner who subsequently worked with Crick; Orgel himself also worked with Crick at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]].<ref>Olby, Robert, ''Francis Crick: Hunter of Life's Secrets,'' Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press, 2009, Chapter 10, p. 181 {{ISBN|978-0-87969-798-3}}</ref>

In 1955 he joined the chemistry department at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]]. There he did work in [[transition metal]] chemistry and [[ligand field theory]], published several peer-reviewed journal articles, and wrote a textbook entitled ''Transition Metal Chemistry: Ligand Field Theory'' (1960). He developed the [[Orgel diagram]] showing the energies of electronic terms in transition metal complexes.

Orgel formulated his [[protein translation|protein-translation]] error-catastrophe theory of aging in 1963,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Orgel |first1=Leslie E. |title=The maintenance of the accuracy of protein synthesis and its relevance to ageing |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA |date=1963 |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=517–521|doi=10.1073/pnas.49.4.517 |pmid=13940312 |pmc=299893 |bibcode=1963PNAS...49..517O |doi-access=free }}</ref> (prior to the use of the term by [[Manfred Eigen]] for mutational [[error catastrophe]]) which has since been experimentally challenged.<ref>{{cite book|title=Evolutionary Biology of Aging|url=https://archive.org/details/evolutionarybiol0000rose|url-access=registration|date=1991|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|location=New York, NY|pages=[https://archive.org/details/evolutionarybiol0000rose/page/147 147–152]|author1=Michael R. Rose|isbn=978-0-19-506133-8 |author-link1=Michael R. Rose}}</ref>

In 1964, Orgel was appointed senior fellow and research professor at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] in [[La Jolla, California]], where he directed the Chemical Evolution Laboratory. He was also an adjunct professor in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at the [[University of California, San Diego]], and he was one of five principal investigators in the [[NASA]]-sponsored NSCORT program in [[Astrobiology|exobiology]]. Orgel also participated in NASA's [[Viking program|Viking]] Mars Lander Program as a member of the Molecular Analysis Team that designed the [[gas chromatography]] [[Mass spectrometry|mass spectrometer]] instrument that robots took to the planet [[Mars]].

Orgel's lab came across an economical way to make [[Cytosine arabinoside|cytarabine]], a compound that is one of today's most commonly used [[Cancer#Treatment|anti-cancer agents]].

Together with [[Stanley Miller]], Orgel also suggested that [[peptide nucleic acid]]s – rather than [[ribonucleic acid]]s – constituted the first pre-[[Life|biotic]] systems capable of [[self-replication]] on [[early Earth]].

His name is popularly known because of [[Orgel's rule]]s, credited to him, particularly Orgel's Second Rule: "[[Evolution]] is cleverer than you are."<ref>{{cite journal|author=Dunitz, Jack D.|author2=Joyce, Gerald F.|title=Leslie E. Orgel|journal=Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences|year=2013|page= 11|url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Orgel_Leslie.pdf}}</ref>

In his book ''The Origins of Life'', Orgel coined the concept of [[specified complexity]], to describe the criterion by which living organisms are distinguished from non-living matter. He published over three hundred articles in his research areas.

In 1993, Orgel presented at the "What is Life?" Conference at [[Trinity College, Dublin|Trinity College]] in Dublin, Ireland along with many other prominent scientists exploring the origin of life research such as [[Manfred Eigen]], [[John Maynard Smith]] and [[Stephen Jay Gould]]. Orgel's talk was on "Molecular Structure and Disordered Crystals."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://icr.provocation.net/whatislf.htm|title=WHAT IS LIFE? The next fifty years Trinity College, Dublin, Ireland September 20th – 22nd|last=Rice|first=Fredric L.|website=icr.provocation.net|access-date=18 November 2016}}</ref>

Orgel died of pancreatic cancer on 27 October 2007 at the San Diego Hospice & Palliative Care in [[San Diego, California]].

== Research on the origin of life==

=== Nucleobase synthesis ===
Orgel proposed a novel solution to a problem with [[Joan Oró|Juan Oro]]'s proposed mechanism of [[nucleobase]] synthesis on the [[Abiogenesis|early Earth]], which relied on the reaction of five molecules of [[hydrogen cyanide]] (HCN) to form [[adenine]]. The problem with this was that it would require much more concentrated hydrogen cyanide than evidence suggested was present.

Orgel suggested that the hydrogen cyanide was frozen in solution.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sanchez|first1=R.|last2=Ferris|first2=J.|last3=Orgel|first3=L. E.|date=1 July 1966|title=Conditions for purine synthesis: did prebiotic synthesis occur at low temperatures?|journal=Science|volume=153|issue=3731|pages=72–73|issn=0036-8075|pmid=5938419|doi=10.1126/science.153.3731.72|bibcode=1966Sci...153...72S|s2cid=31527498}}</ref> This would concentrate HCN molecules in the spaces in between the [[Crystal structure|crystal lattice]] of ice, and also solve the problem of HCN being too [[Volatile organic compound|volatile]] in a liquid water solution.

=== Nucleoside formation ===
For [[nucleoside]] ([[nucleobase]] + [[ribose]] sugar) synthesis, Orgel suggested an almost opposite approach, heating a mixture of ribose and the [[purine]] nucleobases [[hypoxanthine]], adenine, and [[guanine]] to dryness in the presence of [[magnesium]] ions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fuller|first1=William D.|last2=Sanchez|first2=Robert A.|last3=Orgel|first3=Leslie E.|date=14 June 1972|title=Studies in prebiotic synthesis|journal=Journal of Molecular Biology|volume=67|issue=1|pages=25–33|doi=10.1016/0022-2836(72)90383-X|pmid=4339529}}</ref> This reaction puts the [[glycosidic bond]] in the correct position in two ways: the nucleobase attaches to the correct carbon on ribose, and in the correct orientation (the beta [[anomer]]).

However, the synthesis was later criticised because it only worked most with hypoxanthine, a nucleobase that is not relevant to current life on Earth, and because it was not specific for the ribose sugar and could instead be applied to other sugars.

=== RNA polymerization ===
Continuing his work studying the [[Abiogenesis#Chemical synthesis|prebiotic synthesis]] of [[RNA]], Orgel explored mechanisms by which inorganic phosphate<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lohrmann|first1=R.|last2=Orgel|first2=Leslie|year=1968|title=Prebiotic Synthesis: Phosphorylation in Aqueous Solution|journal=Science|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|volume=161|issue=3836|pages=64–66|jstor=1724394|doi=10.1126/science.161.3836.64|pmid=5655266|bibcode=1968Sci...161...64L|s2cid=13005451}}</ref> and nucleotide [[phosphoryl group]]s<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Weimann|first1=B.|last2=Lohrmann|first2=R.|last3=Orgel|first3=Leslie|last4=Schneider-Bernloher|first4=H.|last5=Sulston|first5=J.|year=1968|title=Template-Directed Synthesis with Adenosine-5'-Phosphorimidazolide|journal=Science|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|volume=161|issue=3839|page=387|jstor=1724244|doi=10.1126/science.161.3839.387|pmid=5661298|bibcode=1968Sci...161..387W|s2cid=35649008}}</ref> could be chemically activated for [[Condensation reaction|condensation]] into nucleic acid polymers. Starting in the 1960s, Orgel explored a variety of cyanide-based activating agents which could have plausibly been present on a young earth. A [[carbodiimide]] reagent was found to be effective at activating nucleotide [[phosphoryl group]]s and promoting the formation of short Adenosine dimers and trimers.<ref name=":3" /> In 2018, John D. Sutherland and co-workers proposed that [[methyl isocyanide]] and [[acetaldehyde]] could combine to form a pre-biotic phosphate activating agent which could plausibly have formed under early-earth conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mariani|first1=Angelica|last2=Russell|first2=David|last3=Javelle|first3=Thomas|last4=Sutherland|first4=John|year=2018|title=A Light-Releasable Potentially Prebiotic Nucleotide Activating Agent|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=140|issue=28|pages=8657–8661|doi=10.1021/jacs.8b05189|pmid=29965757|pmc=6152610|doi-access=free|bibcode=2018JAChS.140.8657M }}</ref>

Orgel also theorised that one single strand of RNA could have been the [[Template strand|template]] for the first life on Earth and that these [[Phosphorimidazolide|imidazole-activated nucleotides]] could have used this RNA template strand to polymerise and [[Replicate (biology)|replicate]]. Lohrmann and Orgel reported that the [[phosphorimidazolide]] derivative of adenosine monophosphate (in which a phosphoryl group oxygen is substituted by an imidazole ring) forms short adenosine oligomers in the presence of poly-uridine templates.<ref name=":1" /> They further discovered that the divalent metal cation used to catalyze the reaction influenced the [[regiochemistry]] of the inter-nucleotide linkage.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Lohrmann|first1=R.|last2=Bridson|first2=P.|last3=Orgel|first3=Leslie|year=1980|title=Efficient Metal-Ion Catalyzed Template-Directed Oligonucleotide Synthesis|journal=Science|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|volume=208|issue=4451|pages=1464–1465|jstor=1684687|doi=10.1126/science.6247762|pmid=6247762|bibcode=1980Sci...208.1464L}}</ref> Pb<sup>2+</sup> gave primarily 5'-2' linked nucleotides while Zn<sup>2+</sup> gave primarily 5'-3' linked nucleotides from guanosine phosphorimidazolides in the presence of a poly-cytidine template. [[Montmorillonite]] clay was also shown to promote the polymerization of adenosine phosphorimidazolide into oligonucleotides tens of bases in length starting from a poly-adenosine 10-mer primer.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ferris|first1=James|last2=Hill|first2=Aubrey|last3=Liu|first3=Rihe|last4=Orgel|first4=Leslie|year=1996|title=Synthesis of Long Prebiotic Oligomers on Mineral Surfaces|journal=Nature|volume=381|issue=6577|pages=59–61|doi=10.1038/381059a0|pmid=8609988|bibcode=1996Natur.381...59F|hdl=2060/19980119839|s2cid=4351826|hdl-access=free}}</ref> In the absence of [[montmorillonite]], the primer was capped through the formation of a 5' adenosine [[pyrophosphate]].

The oligonucleotide products in early studies were typically characterized through a combination of <sup>14</sup>C [[Isotopic labeling|radiolabeling]], [[Gel electrophoresis of nucleic acids|gel electrophoresis]], and paper [[electrophoresis]]. Enzymatic digestion was used to differentiate [[regioisomer]]s.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Sulston|first1=J.|last2=Lohrmann|first2=R.|last3=Orgel|first3=Leslie|last4=Miles|first4=H.|title=Nonenzymatic Synthesis of Oligoadenylates on a Polyuridie Acid Template|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=59|issue=3|pages=726–733|doi=10.1073/pnas.59.3.726|pmid=5238657|pmc=224735|year=1968|bibcode=1968PNAS...59..726S|doi-access=free}}</ref> The advent of [[High-performance liquid chromatography|HPLC]] allowed the characterization of long oligomers of guanosine.<ref name=":2" />

=== Directed panspermia ===
Though he later downplayed the hypothesis, Orgel, along with [[Francis Crick]], proposed a detailed [[panspermia]] scenario for the origin of life on Earth, going so far as to suggest that life on Earth was designed by an [[Extraterrestrial life|alien species]] and sent to Earth.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Crick|first1=F. H. C.|last2=Orgel|first2=L. E.|date=1 July 1973|title=Directed panspermia|journal=Icarus|volume=19|issue=3|pages=341–346|doi=10.1016/0019-1035(73)90110-3|bibcode=1973Icar...19..341C}}</ref> They proposed a design for the spaceship that aliens could have used to seed life on Earth.

=== RNA world ===
In the late 1960s, Orgel proposed that life was based on RNA before it was based on DNA or proteins. His theory included genes based on RNA and RNA enzymes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Joyce|first=Gerald F.|year=2007|title=Obituary: Leslie Orgel (1927–2007)|journal=Nature|volume=450|issue=7170|page=627|doi=10.1038/450627a|pmid=18046392|bibcode=2007Natur.450..627J|s2cid=5439488 }}</ref> This view would be developed and shaped into the now widely accepted [[RNA world]] hypothesis.

Almost thirty years later, Orgel wrote a lengthy review of the RNA World hypothesis.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Orgel|first=Leslie E|date=1 January 2004|title=Prebiotic Chemistry and the Origin of the RNA World|journal=Critical Reviews in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology|volume=39|issue=2|pages=99–123|doi=10.1080/10409230490460765|issn=1040-9238|pmid=15217990|s2cid=4939632 }}</ref> This review highlighted many proposed syntheses for RNA and its parts in [[Abiotic component|abiotic]] conditions, noted the significance of the discovery of [[ribozyme]]s (RNA molecules that function as [[enzyme]]s just as Orgel had once predicted) and at the same time, demonstrated nucleic acid polymers with alternatives to ribose such as [[Threose nucleic acid|threose nucleic acid (TNA)]] and [[Peptide nucleic acid|peptide nucleic acid (PNA)]].

In conclusion, Orgel wrote, "One must recognize that, despite considerable progress, the problem of the origin of the RNA World is far from being solved."<ref name=":0" />
